scope.industry: Residential heat pumps, with emphasis on installation and aftercare
scope.interpretation: Includes residential air-to-water, ground-source and air-to-air equipment, installation and aftercare. Excludes industrial and district-heating projects and standalone fossil-fuel boilers. For the installer roll-up angle, installed-project spending is more relevant than manufacturer revenue. Wider European company figures are explicitly labelled and are not EU market shares.

bottom_line: This is both an equipment market and a local installation/service industry. For a roll-up, distinguish household project revenue from manufacturer sales: they are different revenue pools, not additive market segments. [S1][S2]

Published estimates span EUR 14.0bn for EU residential equipment in 2024 to EUR 22.5bn for equipment plus installation in 2025. This is a scope-and-year range, not competing estimates of the same market. [S1][S2]
Demand is recovering but policy-sensitive: the Commission reports 2.6m EU heat-pump sales in 2025, up 13%; that broader unit measure is not a verified residential installer revenue total. [S3]

Roll-up thesis—inference: local workforce capacity, installation quality and a simpler customer journey may matter more than purchasing scale alone. The Commission identifies installer shortages, complexity and installation costs as adoption barriers. [S3]

Fragmentation is reported, not independently established: the supplied Observatory page says most installer businesses have fewer than ten employees, without specifying the observation year or methodology. [S2]

Inference: recurring service and integrated home-energy offerings can extend the customer relationship, but financing, guarantees and manufacturing can introduce risks beyond a conventional installer acquisition. [S4][S6][S7]

business_models: Project installation: household spending combines equipment and installation. Diligence inference: separate equipment pass-through from labour contribution, then test technician productivity, subcontracting, customer-acquisition costs and remedial work. The reported typical installation cost share is not an installer profit margin. [S2][S3]

Service and aftercare: maintenance and repair create a continuing operational role. Inference: test service-contract attachment, renewal, route density and warranty reimbursement rather than assuming recurring revenue is automatically profitable. [S4][S6]

Integrated financed offering: Aira combines equipment, installation, monthly payments and a guarantee. Inference: establish who funds the receivable, bears credit risk and pays future guarantee costs; the commercial announcement does not settle those questions. [S6]

Home-energy bundle: 1KOMMA5° combines heat pumps with solar, batteries and intelligent electricity control. Inference: cross-selling may improve acquisition economics, but distinguish installation earnings from software and energy-service earnings. [S7]

Capital and cash: Aira's manufacturing and R&D demonstrate a more capital-intensive model than installation alone. Roll-up diligence inference: model acquisition spending, fleet/tools, training, inventory, deposits, subsidy-linked collections and warranty cash separately; no reliable sector working-capital benchmark was found. trends.trend: Demand recovery remains country- and policy-dependent

trends.trend: Workforce development is part of the competitive model
trends.evidence: The Commission launched its Heat Pump Accelerator Platform in January 2025. Aira reported operating installer-training academies in its August 2025 financing announcement.
trends.implication: Inference: retaining skilled teams and building training capacity may create more durable integration benefits than procurement savings alone.

trends.trend: Funded integrated providers compete beyond equipment price
trends.evidence: On 2025-08-11, Aira announced EUR 150m of equity financing and described monthly payments, end-to-end service and a 15-year guarantee.
trends.implication: Inference: a roll-up needs a clear response on affordability, service and trust, without taking financing or guarantee risk it cannot price.

trends.evidence: In January 2026, 1KOMMA5° described connecting heat pumps, solar and storage through Heartbeat AI and reported more than 10,000 German heat-pump sales during 2024–2025.
trends.implication: Inference: cross-selling and controls are potential differentiators, but require separate evidence of customer savings and incremental profitability.

trends.trend: Building-policy implementation moves to national execution
trends.evidence: The revised EPBD's national transposition deadline was 2026-05-29; the Commission describes country-specific residential renovation trajectories and flexibility over measures.
trends.implication: Inference: acquisition screening must be country-specific; an EU policy direction does not establish a target's immediate addressable backlog.

report_markdown:
# EU residential heat pumps: installer roll-up primer

## Bottom line
- The acquisition thesis is a local installation-and-service business, not simply exposure to equipment growth. Customer complexity, installer shortages and installation costs are documented barriers. **Inference:** execution quality and workforce retention should lead the thesis. [S3]
- Equipment and installed-project market estimates are different revenue measures. Do not add or average them. [S1][S2]
- Fragmentation is reported, but its scale and achievable consolidation benefits remain unverified. [S2]

## Definition and size
Includes residential air-to-water, ground-source and air-to-air systems, installation and aftercare; excludes industrial and district-heating projects. NACE Rev. 2.1 43.22 covers plumbing, heat and air-conditioning installation, substantially broader than this target market; code verified only through a search excerpt. [S1][S3][S5]

| Value | Definition | Data year | Published | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EUR 15.3bn | EU residential manufacturer equipment sales | 2023 | 2026-01-27 | [S1] |
| EUR 14.0bn | Same scope; installation labour excluded | 2024 | 2026-01-27 | [S1] |
| EUR 22.5bn | EU household equipment plus installation spending | 2025 | 2026-06-09 | [S2] |
| 2.6m units | Broader EU demand proxy; up 13% | 2025 | Not stated | [S3] |
| EUR 23bn | Broader EU heat-pump investment proxy | 2023 | March 2024 underlying source | [S3] |
| Not found | Residential installation-only revenue | — | — | [S2][S3] |

The headline EUR 14.0bn–22.5bn span changes both year and revenue boundary. The Observatory's typical-project installation share is not a sector margin or a valid basis for extracting an EU installation market. [S1][S2]

## Value chain and margins
| Stage | Participants | Typical margin |
|---|---|---|
| Equipment | Manufacturers; integrated Aira model | Not found [S6] |
| Acquisition/finance | Installers and integrated providers | Not found [S3][S6] |
| Installation | Local businesses and employed teams | Not found [S2][S6] |
| Aftercare | Qualified service personnel | Not found [S4] |
| Energy optimisation | Connected home-energy platforms | Not found [S7] |

## Business models
Project revenue combines equipment and installation. Service adds a continuing customer relationship; integrated providers also offer financing, guarantees and energy controls. **Diligence inference:** reconcile equipment pass-through, direct labour, acquisition costs and callbacks before attributing value to scale. Model inventory, project cash timing and guarantee liabilities separately. Manufacturing adds capital requirements beyond installation. [S2][S3][S4][S6][S7]

## Key players
Illustrative comparators, not an EU ranking:

| Provider | Position and scale |
|---|---|
| Aira | Investor-backed integrated provider in Germany, Italy and UK; company-reported EUR 200m annual sales run-rate in August 2025, not EU annual revenue. [S6] |
| 1KOMMA5° | Home-energy integrator; reports over 10,000 German heat-pump sales during 2024–2025, not equivalent completed installations. [S7] |

## Metrics
Proposed diligence dashboard; no typical ranges verified:

| KPI | Question |
|---|---|
| Completions/conversion | Do orders become accepted jobs? [S7] |
| Contribution/job | What remains after direct project costs? [S2] |
| Crew productivity | Is scarce labour deployed effectively? [S3] |
| Acquisition cost | What does a completed customer cost? [S3][S6] |
| Callbacks/aftercare | Are guarantees and service profitable? [S4][S6] |
| Cash conversion | When are project receipts collected? [S3][S6] |

## Regulation
F-gas guidance addresses qualifications, emissions, applicable leak checks, records and recovery. The revised EPBD entered into force on 2024-05-28; national transposition was due 2026-05-29. It establishes national residential trajectories, not a universal household heat-pump mandate. Country implementation requires separate checking. [S4][S8]

## Trends
Recent evidence shows 2025 demand recovery, January 2025 workforce-policy coordination, Aira's August 2025 financing, January 2026 integrated-energy positioning and the May 2026 EPBD transposition deadline. **Inference:** prioritise country selection, technician retention, affordability and operational integration over a generic EU growth thesis. [S3][S6][S7][S8]

## Glossary
**Air-to-water:** heats a water circuit; **air-to-air:** heats indoor air; **ground-source:** draws ground heat; **installed spending:** equipment plus installation; **F-gases:** regulated fluorinated gases; **EPBD:** building-performance framework; **run-rate:** annualised trading measure; **virtual power plant:** coordinated connected energy devices. [S1][S2][S3][S4][S6][S7][S8]

## Go deeper
Use Commission heat-pump country-fiche links, F-gas guidance and the EPBD overview before country diligence. [S3][S4][S8]

## Gaps
Supplied valuations lack independent corroboration. Installer fragmentation has no stated observation year. Margins, transaction multiples, ownership details, realised synergies and national licensing/subsidies remain unverified. This is research, not investment, legal or regulatory advice.
